column3: It is the direct parallel account of Satan's whisper, tree, and promise of immortality, adding the deception's stated aim.
Its measured gathering of shadow offers only a distant counterimage to the promised permanence.
It gives the prior prohibition of the very tree that the focus presents as the object of Satan's offer.
It directly precedes the focus by naming the speaker an enemy and warning Adam against the resulting expulsion.
The accusation about Musa driving people from their land does not clarify Satan's offer to Adam.
Its enduring punishment supplies a contrary instance of real permanence, though outside the Adam scene.
It repeats the command not to approach the tree, but adds less after the closer parallel at 7:19.
The extension and stillness of shadow only broadly contrasts with an unwearing possession.
It qualifies lasting residence as subject to God's will, countering any autonomous claim to permanence.
It identifies Satan as a manifest human enemy, a useful but non-Adam parallel to the warning in the focus.
It immediately establishes Adam's secure provision in the garden, which Satan misrepresents as lacking.
Its protective plant is a different use of a tree and adds little to the deceptive tree motif.
It explicitly denies immortality to human beings, directly exposing the false premise of the offer.
The command to listen to revelation only distantly contrasts with heeding a whisper.
It treats hidden whispering as known to God, extending the focus's concealed mode of influence.
The tree of Zaqqqum supplies a negative tree contrast, but it is not tied to Adam's temptation.
Its assertion that revelation is serious does not add a focused link.
It names the recurrent withdrawing whisperer, a broad but clear counterpart to Satan's whisper here.
It gives the immediate outcome of the deception: tasting the tree, exposure, and confirmation of Satan's enmity.
It completes the garden's lack of thirst and exposure, clarifying the sufficiency Satan's offer contests.
The oath made under a tree does not illuminate the deceptive tree or false permanence.
Its offer to indicate a nursing household shares only an ordinary guidance formula.
Musa's staff does not clarify the whisper, tree, or claimed dominion.
Its lasting punishment is a distant contrast to the permanence offered in the focus.
It locates whispering within human breasts, extending the hidden mechanism but not the Adam narrative.
The garden owners' test is too different from the prohibited tree to add much.
Its enduring fire offers only a repeated, contrary form of permanence.
The offer of a saving trade is not a useful parallel to Satan's deceptive offer.
It is the next ayah: Adam and his wife eat from the tree and the disobedience's consequence appears.
Its enduring youths provide only a remote image of permanence.
The tree rooted in Hell forms a meaningful negative contrast to the tree advertised as the route to permanence.
Musa's request to loosen his tongue is unrelated.
Its enduring burden concerns the Hereafter, not the false promise made to Adam.
The promised garden of permanence provides a genuine divine counterpart to Satan's counterfeit route to permanence.
Testing reports does not clarify the temptation scene.
Its lasting fire is a general contrary permanence statement with little marginal value.
Adam's divinely given knowledge and disclosure of the hidden form a useful contrast to Satan's misleading speech.
Its high ranks for the faithful lead into the true lasting garden described in the following ayah.
Its eternal garden is another general image of genuine permanence, largely redundant with earlier cards.
It calls Satan a manifest, misleading enemy, reinforcing the enemy warning that frames the focus.
The fate of prior communities does not clarify the whisper or its promise.
Its enduring attendants add only a remote picture of permanence.
It assigns all dominion to God, directly contrasting Satan's offer of an unwearing dominion.
The restoration of Musa's staff to its former condition only lightly resonates with the claim that something will not wear out.
Its false equivalence and Satanic disorientation give a distant pattern of deceptive framing.
The punishment called lasting is a general contrary permanence statement.
Degrees according to deeds do not clarify the focus.
Its competing patrons and movement between light and darkness only broadly resemble misdirection.
Satan beautifies a course, promises security, then abandons its followers, closely paralleling deceptive reassurance.
It gives a true lasting garden, but adds little beyond the earlier genuine-permanence parallels.
The Day of Permanence names a genuine, divinely granted lasting state that contrasts with Satan's promise.
The lasting abode of fire is another broad contrary permanence image.
The instruction not to weaken does not illuminate the focus.
It exposes building as an attempt to secure lasting existence, a close analogue to seeking permanence through a material means.
Its lasting punishment repeats the contrary eternity theme without adding to the temptation's mechanism.
Deliverance from an enemy and provision in the same surah offer only broad contextual resonance.
Its permanent residence in Hell is a further general contrary instance of permanence.
Trees as pens for inexhaustible divine words do not clarify the deceptive tree's function.
The contrast between knowing truth and blindness is too general here.
Its enduring gardens repeat a genuine permanence motif already represented.
The approach to Ibrahim does not add a focused connection.
Patient praise in response to hostile speech only distantly contrasts with the satanic utterance.
Its nourishing tree is a different tree motif with little relation to counterfeit permanence.
Mistaking temporary ease for divine honor provides a loose analogue to a misleading valuation of provision.
Its commands about permission and obedience do not clarify the focus.
The promised lasting fire is a repetitive contrary permanence statement.
The skeptical question about re-creation is a distant example of misleading speech, not the focus's promise.
It identifies fabricated magic as a failed deception, a useful nearby contrast to Satan's persuasive stratagem.
Its eternal garden restates genuine permanence with little new marginal value.
Its contrast between ownership and provision only broadly relates to the offered dominion.
It begins the immediate Adam sequence by recalling his covenant, forgetfulness, and lack of resolve before the whisper.
Its good permanent dwelling is another general genuine-permanence counterpart.
The blessed tree in the parable of light is not a focused counterpart to the forbidden tree.
Faith and striving describe the true saving trade, not the focus's deception.
Its lasting enjoyment is a remote image of genuine permanence.
Unseen divine nearness does not clarify Satan's whisper.
The sanctity of Musa's valley is unrelated.
Its permanent punishment is another general contrast with the promised immortality.
False claims before God and their judgment give a broad contrast to Satan's false speech.
The exposure of secrets lightly relates to hidden whispering, but adds no Adam-specific link.
Its eternal fire is redundant general contrary permanence evidence.
The request for a king gives only a distant contrast to the promised dominion.
Inheritance of an eternal garden restates genuine permanence without clarifying the deception.
Hidden thoughts and mistaken assumptions offer a limited parallel to concealed suggestion.
The prostration of plants and trees does not add to the temptation's tree.
Its declaration of signs and testing is too general.
It treats a tree as a created bearer of hidden potential, a secondary contrast to treating one as the source of permanence.
The manifest test statement does not clarify the focus.
It directly portrays the false assumption that wealth can make someone immortal, closely matching the lure of permanence.
It warns against serving Satan because of his rebellion, a useful general account of the deceiver's character.
It attributes a false story to self-persuasion, offering a secondary pattern of deceptive internal prompting.
Musa's flight and prayer for rescue do not clarify the focus.
The command to address disbelievers has no focused relation.
Its false speech and inward concealment only broadly resemble deceptive utterance.
A questioned false claim and God's knowledge of what is hidden offer a useful contrast to deceptive speech, though in another scene.
Its proof of resurrection through creation and growth only distantly relates to enduring life.
The command to return to worldly comforts does not clarify the temptation.
Its hushed speech is a distinct eschatological whisper and adds only a lexical parallel.
The command to fear God and obey does not clarify the focus.
Its tree contains a hidden capacity contrary to its appearance, a secondary parallel to the tree's deceptively assigned function.
Satan reinforces his tree-and-immortality claim with a false oath of sincere counsel, exposing the persuasive layer omitted from the focus.
It gives the parallel result of Satan's causing Adam and his wife to slip and leave the garden after the prohibited tree.
It directly recalls Satan's stripping Adam and his wife of their covering and driving them from the garden, tying whisper to consequence.
It supplies the immediate divine response after Adam's lapse: election, repentance, and guidance rather than the permanence Satan advertised.
It continues the immediate sequence with descent, reciprocal enmity, and the promise that following divine guidance prevents going astray.
Adam and his wife acknowledge their wrong and seek mercy, providing the repentant response to the temptation.
It gives the parallel account of Adam receiving words and being accepted in repentance after the lapse.
It pairs descent with the promise that following divine guidance removes fear and grief, contrasting the whisper's false route.
It gives the descent from the garden and the new earthly term of dwelling, a direct consequence of the temptation.
Turning away from divine remembrance brings constricted life and resurrection, extending the warning opposed to following the whisper.
It says Satan promises and arouses desire but his promise is only delusion, directly characterizing the focus's offer.
It describes Satan's voice, inducement, and promises, then explicitly calls those promises delusion, closely explaining his tactic toward Adam.
Satan later admits that he merely invited people with a promise he broke, a decisive retrospective contrast to his offer in the focus.
Satan declares that he will make evil attractive on earth and lead people astray, clarifying the strategy embodied in the whisper.
Satan vows to sit on God's straight path for people, showing the active opposition behind the offer.
It expands Satan's vowed approach from every direction and his aim of producing ingratitude, supplying his broader program.
Satan protests Adam's honor and vows to bring Adam's descendants under his control, directly continuing the Adam conflict.
Satan swears by divine might that he will mislead all people, a broad but important declaration of the deceiver's intent.
It identifies Iblis's disobedience and warns against taking him and his progeny as patrons, giving necessary background to his enmity.
It commands people to treat Satan as an enemy because he calls his party toward the Fire, reinforcing the warning given Adam.
The covenant not to worship Satan and the designation of him as a manifest enemy generalize the focus's warning.
Satan prompts disbelief and then disowns the person, a later pattern of inducement followed by abandonment.
It limits Satan's authority over those who believe and rely on their Lord, offering a protective counterpart to his whisper.
Satan causes people to forget God's remembrance, a secondary parallel to the focus's setting of Adam's forgetfulness.
